{{Short description|American mathematician (1931–2017)}}
'''Leonard Esau Baum''' (August 23, 1931 – August 14, 2017) was an American mathematician, known for the [[Baum–Welch algorithm]] and [[Baum–Sweet sequence]]. He graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1953,<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.thecrimson.com/article/1952/11/24/pbk-chooses-sixteen-from-class-of/|title=PBK Chooses Sixteen from Class of '53|journal=[[The Harvard Crimson]]|date=November 24, 1952}}.</ref> and earned a Ph.D. in mathematics from Harvard in 1958, with a dissertation titled ''Derivations in Commutative Semi-Simple Banach Algebras''.<ref>[http://www.math.harvard.edu/dissertations/index.html Harvard Mathematics Dissertations] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404132750/http://www.math.harvard.edu/dissertations/index.html |date=2019-04-04 }}, accessed 2013-01-13.</ref> 

He developed the Baum–Welch Algorithm with [[Lloyd R. Welch|Lloyd Welch]] while working for the [[Institute_for_Defense_Analyses#Center_for_Communications_and_Computing|Communications Research Division of IDA]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/First-Hand:The_Hidden_Markov_Model|title=First-Hand:The Hidden Markov Model|first=Lawrence R.|last=Rabiner|author-link=Lawrence Rabiner|publisher=IEEE Global History Network|access-date=2013-01-13}}</ref> It enabled the development of [[speech recognition]] and had applications in [[cryptanalysis]] and [[genetics]].  He coined the motto of the Communications Research Division: "Bad ideas is good, good ideas is terrific, no ideas is terrible."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.usgo.org/news/2018/06/in-memoriam-leonard-baum/|title=In Memoriam: Leonard Baum|website=American Go E-Journal|language=en-US|access-date=2018-06-19|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003210708/https://www.usgo.org/news/2018/06/in-memoriam-leonard-baum/|archive-date=2022-10-03}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YUmHDwAAQBAJ&q=lenny+baum+no+idea+is+bad+jim+simons&pg=PA25|title=The Man Who Solved the Market: How Jim Simons Launched the Quant Revolution|last=Zuckerman|first=Gregory|date=2019-11-05|publisher=Penguin|isbn=978-0-7352-1799-7|pages=25|language=en}}</ref> 

Later, in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Baum used mathematical models for [[Foreign exchange market|currency trading]], working with [[Renaissance Technologies#Monemetrics|Monemetrics]], a predecessor of [[hedge fund]] management company [[Renaissance Technologies]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601213&sid=aq33M3X795vQ&refer=home|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071202081120/https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601213&sid=aq33M3X795vQ&refer=home|url-status=dead|archive-date=2007-12-02|title=Simons at Renaissance Cracks Code, Doubling Assets |last=Teitelbaum|first=Richard |date=2008-10-27|publisher=Bloomberg|access-date=2009-06-02}}</ref> He left the firm in 1984 amid steep losses.<ref name=":1" /> In his later years, he would participate in [[Go (game)|Go]] tournaments and work on mathematical problems relating to prime numbers and the Riemann hypothesis.<ref name=":0" /> He died at his home in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], on August 14, 2017, at the age of 86.<ref name=":0" />
